title.narrative: Activity under preparation Enhanced Access to Justice in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

description.narrative: Contract related to: Enhanced Access to Justice in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa - Enhancing Commercial Dispute Resolution (CDR) is a pre-condition for Global Gateway investments in Pakistan. Although Pakistan has a nominally open foreign direct investment regime, it remains a challenging environment for investors. Challenges with rule of law in general and commercial dispute resolution in particular are irritants for business development and notably for EU private sector investments in Pakistan. Costly and lengthy court and arbitration processes, as well as limited enforcement of arbitral awards, hinder businesses, especially Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs), from scaling and formalising. Cognisant of this, Pakistan has started to revise legislation in the area of commercial law. The emergence, in the last five years, of provincial ADR laws and landmark rulings promoting the recourse of mediation and arbitration in corporate disputes, is marking a significant step forward for the use of ADR in the trade and private-sector development. Key challenges include the following: Fragmented regulatory framework: Although ADR legal frameworks were updated, they still vary across federal, provincial, and local levels, creating unpredictability for businesses. For instance, unlike Punjab, Sindh does not have dedicated commercial courts. Outcome 1 will address this issue towards enhanced coherence at national level.Outdated/complex judicial processes: The judicial system still relies heavily on manual case management and outdated procedures, resulting in inefficiencies that discourage formal contract use and impede access to redress. Commercial cases are processed alongside a high volume of general civil disputes¿approximately 50¿80%¿clogging the system and diverting judicial attention and resources away from commercial matters.Limited awareness and capacity among key stakeholders: Many businesses¿particularly SMEs¿lack understanding of formal dispute resolution options, including the potential advantages of ADR. Commercial court judges, arbitrators, and mediators often do not receive training in commercial law and dispute resolution techniques.Inefficiencies of the regulatory bodies: Gaps in mandates and capacities of regulatory bodies tend to hinder smooth business operations. These inefficiencies include delays in company registrations, ineffective handling of disputes, and inefficiencies in addressing complaints from SMEs against larger market players, amongst others.Weak public-private coordination: Mechanisms for dialogue between the judiciary, legal sector, and private sector actors¿especially SMEs¿are limited. As a result, the development and implementation of commercial justice reforms often do not reflect the needs of businesses.
